analysis.one_liner: Bars H-2A farm workers from suing employers anywhere except the employer's home state.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House Judiciary subcommittee after being introduced with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: H-2A visas bring foreign workers to the U.S. for temporary farm jobs. This bill would change federal law so that an H-2A worker who wanted to sue an employer — over wages, injuries, or anything else arising from the job — could only file the case in the state where the employer lives or has its main place of business. Practically, that often means a worker in one state would have to travel to another state, hire lawyers there, and fight the case on the employer's home turf. The bill was introduced in April 2000 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which sent it to its immigration subcommittee; nothing further happened before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Agricultural employers who use H-2A workers. Facing a lawsuit in the employer's own home state raises the cost and inconvenience of suing for the worker, and lowers the practical chance that an employer is sued at all — especially by low-wage workers far from home.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the H-2A visa program (Section 218 of the Immigration and Nationality Act) to forbid a worker from bringing any state or federal claim arising out of H-2A employment except in the state where the employer resides or has its principal place of business. [S2] [S3]
For farm employers, this means any lawsuit filed against them arrives in a courthouse near their own home or headquarters, where they and their lawyers already operate. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: H-2A guest workers. A worker injured or shortchanged on the job would generally have to sue in the employer's home state rather than where the work happened, adding travel, legal, and practical barriers for people who are typically low-wage and away from home.
analysis.who_pays_short: H-2A guest workers seeking to sue

drawbacks.text: Employers had a genuine complaint that venue rules let workers sue far from the employer's home, forcing farmers to defend cases in distant states with unfamiliar courts and higher defense costs. [S3]

The strongest honest objection from the worker's side: as drafted, the bill offered no offsetting protection — it was a one-way rule that applied to every claim under state or federal law arising from H-2A employment, with no exception for where the injury occurred. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The employer-side concern about defending suits far from home is real, but the bill solved it entirely on the employer's side: it placed the entire burden on the worker, who must now litigate in the employer's home state under a rule overriding 'any other provision of law.' For low-wage guest workers, that burden is heavy enough to make many valid claims impractical to bring.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to its immigration subcommittee, and then sat there until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Whitfield of Kentucky introduced the bill on April 13, 2000. [S1] [S5]
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary. [S5]
On April 25, 2000, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Immigration and Claims, and no further action was taken before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: H-2A workers kept their existing ability to sue employers where their claims arise; agricultural employers gained nothing but lost a chance to shift lawsuits to their home states.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: H-2A workers kept their access to courts

for.name: Rep. Ed Whitfield
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Subcommittee on Immigration and Claims
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Immigration and Claims and took no further action, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a vote or a cosponsor, so no party positions were ever recorded; its single sponsor was a Republican.

industries.industry: Agricultural employers using H-2A guest workers
industries.note: The bill would have made it harder and costlier for their workers to sue them by forcing cases into the employer's home state. The industry's gain in litigation convenience came directly out of workers' access to the courts.
